query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Premelting and melting in iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are governed by differential surface segregation driven by thermally activated atomic diffusion. In particular, the lower melting point and higher mobility of copper cause it to migrate to the nanoparticle surface, forming a premelted, liquid‐like layer that softens the particle and triggers subsequent bulk melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Initially solid, single-phase HEA nanoparticles with a nearly homogeneous elemental distribution of iron, nickel, chromium, cobalt, and copper.
generation.intervention: Controlled in situ heating of the nanoparticles from ambient temperature through the premelting regime up to full melting.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under high-vacuum or controlled atmosphere conditions (e.g., in situ STEM heating) with temperature increments spanning room temperature to just above the melt point of the alloy nanoparticles; nanoparticle size in the tens-of-nanometer range where surface effects are significant.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a copper-enriched surface layer resulting from differential atomic mobilities and surface energies.
generation.mechanism: Thermal energy activates diffusion among constituent elements. Given copper’s lower melting point and relatively weaker bonding, it segregates to the nanoparticle surface under heating conditions. This leads to a localized premelted, liquid-like layer that acts as a mediator, reducing the effective melting temperature of the particle and initiating a stepwise melting process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Before complete melting, in situ imaging and compositional mapping will reveal a gradual development of a copper-enriched, liquid-like surface layer. This premelted layer will form at a temperature lower than that of homogeneous monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles lacking such pronounced segregation.
generation.baseline: Monometallic nanoparticles or simpler bimetallic systems where similar differential surface diffusion is not present, and where premelting does not involve marked elemental segregation.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles of equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys in the tens-of-nanometers size regime. It is expected to hold when surface energy effects dominate and under heating conditions that allow sufficient atomic mobility without inducing other competing effects (e.g., oxidation).
generation.uncertainty: The exact onset temperature of copper segregation, the thickness of the premelted layer, and the influence of nanoparticle size and local environmental factors remain uncertain and may vary between samples.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ STEM heating experiments on the iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles while concurrently mapping the elemental composition across the nanoparticle at incremental temperatures. Complement the measurements with molecular dynamics simulations to track atomic diffusion and surface composition evolution.
measurements: High-resolution STEM imaging to detect morphological changes indicating a surface liquid layer
Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX) line scans or mapping to trace copper enrichment at the nanoparticle surface
Temperature-dependent diffraction or spectroscopic analyses to monitor phase changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, during the heating process, no preferential enrichment of copper (or another lower melting constituent) is observable at the nanoparticle surface prior to bulk melting, or if the melting transition occurs homogeneously without formation of a premelted surface layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. Here, in situ aberration‐corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) and molecular dynamics simulations are combined to investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles (NPs) from 298 to 973 K. Both in situ STEM heating and atomistic simulations reveal strong structural and chemical evolutions in the NPs with the formation and melting of an AuCu layer at the surface of NPs at high temperature. This phase separation that appears progressively with temperature is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion that is surprisingly more active in these quinary nanoalloys than in monometallic and bimetallic subsystems.
